title: ArborMem: Navigating Interaction States with Memory Forests

visual_explainer.blocker: A paper-specific GPT Image attempt on 2026-08-20 ignored the grounded ArborMem brief and rendered a generic Agent Memory Radar dashboard with fabricated paper metadata. Visual QA rejected the render; no image was published.

analysis.tldr: ArborMem treats long conversations as a forest of interaction states and makes state localization precede evidence retrieval: the agent identifies the branch/state being resumed, restores the branch-local trajectory, then retrieves only supplemental cross-branch facts and records before committing the new state after generation.
analysis.problem: Chronological or globally retrieved memory conflates two questions: which prior interaction state is the user resuming, and what additional evidence is needed once that state is known. Interleaved projects, backjumps, and updates can make topically similar but state-incompatible memories harmful.
analysis.core_idea: Represent interaction history as a forest whose nodes are conversation states. A new turn takes a cue-based fast path when continuation/temporal references are explicit, otherwise retrieves candidate states and reranks them with branch summaries, node summaries, entities, and path context. After choosing a parent, ArborMem restores the branch-local root-to-parent trajectory and retrieves supplemental facts/records across branches; only after responding is the new node and derived state committed.

memory_design.write: After response generation, commit a new interaction-state node plus extracted facts/structured records with provenance and revision metadata; write is deliberately downstream of read/generation.
memory_design.organize: Maintain a forest of interaction-state nodes with parent/branch structure, path/node summaries, topic keys, entities, and supplemental atomic facts/records.
memory_design.read: Localize the resumed parent state first; restore the branch-local trajectory; then retrieve cross-branch supplemental facts/records needed for the current turn.
memory_design.update_forget: New turns extend a branch or create a new one and records can carry revision metadata; explicit deletion/aging and robust branch repair after misrouting are not the focus.

compared_to: Long-term memory baselines on LongMemEval, LoCoMo, BEAM100K, and BranchMemEval
A fixed LongMemEval ablation removing state localization while retaining the rest of the pipeline
Component ablations over atomic-fact retrieval and branch/state machinery
analysis.evidence: ArborMem reports gains over the strongest compared baseline of +9 points on LongMemEval, +10.31 on LoCoMo, +3.36 on BEAM100K, and +5 on BranchMemEval; it is also 15 points above full-context on BranchMemEval. On a fixed 50-question LongMemEval subset, removing state localization drops the 30B model from 82→70 but the 4B model only 48→46; removing atomic-fact retrieval drops the 30B setting further to 62. This supports state localization as a real but not sole contributor.
analysis.why_it_matters: ArborMem exposes a read-side boundary that ordinary retrieval collapses: before asking which memories are relevant, an agent may need to decide which historical state is currently active. That suggests future long-horizon memory systems should evaluate state localization separately from evidence retrieval.
limitations: The full system changes branch representation, facts/records, prompting, and retrieval together; the package evidence is stronger than attribution to the forest alone.
The state-localization ablation is model-dependent and small for the 4B setting.
BranchMemEval is small and synthetic, and many cases remain within ordinary context windows.
The single-parent state model is awkward for genuinely multi-intent turns; routing errors can also propagate into later branch structure.
